source_guideline.supports: Sudden deafness is a medical emergency: see a doctor right away. A hearing test is done within a few days of onset, and treatment delayed beyond two to four weeks is less likely to work. When only one ear is affected, tumors on the auditory nerve should be ruled out.
source_guideline.title: NIDCD (US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders): Sudden deafness

turns.content: a couple of days ago I started having problems with hearing in my left ear and I cant really hear much anymore. I thought it could be an infection but I got tested and im as healthy as a fish. Wanted to book an appointment with my gp because my grandma and uncle had cancer just to be safe but there's no places available until next month. Can it wait?

Check for availability today or tomorrow at the latest with other doctors or in the private sector. If nothing is available, go to the ER, because sudden deafness is not a symptom to be taken lightly and one of the possible causes is a tumor on the auditory nerve.

but im just 20, there's no way I have a tumor. Plus, I feel fine in everything else, even my blood tests came up nice and clean. i dont want to spend hours in the er for a hunch. I'll just wait for whichever availability my gp has next

response:
It is completely understandable to feel hesitant about going to the ER, especially when you are young, feeling otherwise well, and have clean blood work. However, **sudden hearing loss in one ear is considered a medical emergency.** 

While the vast majority of causes are not tumors, time is the single most critical factor in preserving your hearing. For certain common causes of sudden sensorineural hearing loss—such as viral infections or severe inflammation of the cochlea—treatments like corticosteroids are most effective **within the first 7 to 14 days**. Waiting a month for a GP appointment means that window of opportunity will likely close, and any hearing loss you have could become permanent.

Furthermore, blood tests generally do not detect issues related to inner ear or nerve function, which is why your results came back normal. 

You do not need to go into this immediately assuming the worst-case scenario, but you do need an urgent evaluation by an Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) specialist or an urgent care facility equipped to perform a formal hearing test (audiometry) right away. 

**Recommended steps:**
1. **Call your GP back** and explicitly state that you are experiencing *sudden, unilateral (one-sided) hearing loss*. Clinics often hold emergency or same-day appointment slots for acute symptoms like this, even if their routine booking calendar is full.
2. **Contact local urgent care centers** or private ENT clinics to see if they can accommodate you much sooner than next month.
3. **Go to an emergency department or urgent care center** if you cannot secure an appointment within the next day or two. While waiting for hours is frustrating, losing your hearing permanently is a risk that is not worth taking. 

To help provide more relevant information, how many days ago did the hearing loss start? Also, have you noticed any other symptoms, like ringing in the ear, dizziness, or a feeling of fullness?
